    1 · Text as a graph¶

    A bag-of-words classifier looks at each document on its own. TextGCN (Yao et al., 2019) takes a different view. The whole corpus becomes one graph, whose nodes are the documents and the words, and a Graph Convolutional Network learns by passing information along its edges.

    Before training anything on a real dataset, we build that graph for twelve sentences and open it up. By the end you will know what nodes and edges Text4GCN creates, and why an unlabelled document can be classified just from its position in the graph.

    Runs on CPU in a few seconds.

    A tiny corpus¶

    Two topics, space and cooking, with five labelled training sentences each. The two test sentences have labels too, but the model will never see them: we only use them to check the predictions at the end.

    save_corpus writes the two files Text4GCN reads: toy.txt, with one document per line, and toy.meta, with <id>\t<train|test>\t<label>.

    Step 1: preprocess¶

    TextPipeline lower-cases and tokenizes the text and removes stop words. It also drops words seen fewer than rare_count times; with twelve sentences we keep every word, so rare_count=1. It then shuffles the documents and saves the vocabulary.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    TextPipeline(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR, rare_count=1).execute()
    TextPipeline(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR, rare_count=1).execute()

    Step 2: build the graph¶

    Frequency.tfidf() builds the original TextGCN graph and saves its adjacency matrix, a scipy.sparse matrix, with pickle. It returns GraphBuildStats, whose path field points to that file.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    stats = Frequency(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR).tfidf()
with open(stats.path, "rb") as f:
    adj = pickle.load(f)
stats
    stats = Frequency(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR).tfidf() with open(stats.path, "rb") as f: adj = pickle.load(f) stats

    Who is who¶

    The adjacency matrix is square: one row per node. The nodes are in a fixed order:

    [ training documents | vocabulary words | test documents ]
    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    train, test = meta[meta.split == "train"], meta[meta.split == "test"]
n_train, n_words = len(train), len(vocab)
assert adj.shape[0] == n_train + n_words + len(test)

nodes = pd.DataFrame({
    "kind": ["train doc"] * n_train + ["word"] * n_words + ["test doc"] * len(test),
    "name": [f"{lb} doc #{i}" for i, lb in zip(train.id, train.label)]
            + vocab
            + [f"? doc #{i}" for i in test.id],
})
nodes.groupby("kind", sort=False).size().rename("nodes")
    train, test = meta[meta.split == "train"], meta[meta.split == "test"] n_train, n_words = len(train), len(vocab) assert adj.shape[0] == n_train + n_words + len(test) nodes = pd.DataFrame({ "kind": ["train doc"] * n_train + ["word"] * n_words + ["test doc"] * len(test), "name": [f"{lb} doc #{i}" for i, lb in zip(train.id, train.label)] + vocab + [f"? doc #{i}" for i in test.id], }) nodes.groupby("kind", sort=False).size().rename("nodes")

    Two kinds of edges¶

    • word–word: two words that co-occur in the same sliding window more often than chance. The weight is their PMI (pointwise mutual information).
    • document–word: a word that occurs in a document. The weight is its TF-IDF.

    There are no document–document edges. Documents only meet through shared words.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    coo = adj.maximum(adj.T).tocoo()   # symmetric: every edge in both directions
edges = pd.DataFrame({"src": nodes.name.values[coo.row], "dst": nodes.name.values[coo.col],
                      "src_kind": nodes.kind.values[coo.row], "dst_kind": nodes.kind.values[coo.col],
                      "weight": coo.data})
edges = edges[coo.row < coo.col]   # each undirected edge once

word_word = edges[(edges.src_kind == "word") & (edges.dst_kind == "word")]
print(f"{len(word_word)} word-word edges; the strongest (PMI):")
# With twelve sentences many pairs tie: they co-occur only in their single sentence.
word_word.nlargest(8, "weight")[["src", "dst", "weight"]]
    coo = adj.maximum(adj.T).tocoo() # symmetric: every edge in both directions edges = pd.DataFrame({"src": nodes.name.values[coo.row], "dst": nodes.name.values[coo.col], "src_kind": nodes.kind.values[coo.row], "dst_kind": nodes.kind.values[coo.col], "weight": coo.data}) edges = edges[coo.row < coo.col] # each undirected edge once word_word = edges[(edges.src_kind == "word") & (edges.dst_kind == "word")] print(f"{len(word_word)} word-word edges; the strongest (PMI):") # With twelve sentences many pairs tie: they co-occur only in their single sentence. word_word.nlargest(8, "weight")[["src", "dst", "weight"]]

    Seeing the structure¶

    We draw the graph with a small force-directed layout: edges pull their nodes together, and all nodes push each other apart. Nothing here has been trained, and labels are used only for the colours.

    Each coloured circle is a document (D7 is document 7), each beige circle a word. A word grows with its number of edges, so the words shared by several documents stand out. Test documents are drawn hollow: the model never sees their label.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    def force_layout(linked: np.ndarray, steps: int = 300, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray:
    """Fruchterman-Reingold: linked nodes attract, every pair of nodes repels."""
    xy = np.random.default_rng(seed).normal(size=(len(linked), 2))
    k = 1 / np.sqrt(len(linked))
    for step in np.linspace(0.1, 0.002, steps):
        delta = xy[:, None] - xy[None, :]
        dist = np.linalg.norm(delta, axis=-1) + 1e-9
        force = ((k**2 / dist**2 - linked * dist / k)[..., None] * delta).sum(axis=1)
        length = np.linalg.norm(force, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9
        xy += force / length * np.minimum(length, step)
    return xy

def remove_overlaps(xy: np.ndarray, radius: np.ndarray, steps: int = 300) -> np.ndarray:
    """Nudge apart every pair of nodes closer than the sum of their radii."""
    for _ in range(steps):
        delta = xy[:, None] - xy[None, :]
        dist = np.linalg.norm(delta, axis=-1) + np.eye(len(xy))
        overlap = np.clip(radius[:, None] + radius[None, :] - dist, 0, None) * (1 - np.eye(len(xy)))
        xy = xy + 0.25 * ((overlap / dist)[..., None] * delta).sum(axis=1)
    return xy

def node_label(k: int) -> str | None:
    """Topic of node k if it is a document (test labels are used only for colouring)."""
    kind = nodes.kind.iloc[k]
    return None if kind == "word" else meta.label.iloc[k if kind == "train doc" else k - n_words]

def draw_document(ax, k: int, xy, size: float = 750) -> None:
    """A document as a circle with its id: filled for training, hollow for test."""
    label, train_doc = node_label(k), nodes.kind.iloc[k] == "train doc"
    ax.scatter(*xy, s=size, zorder=2, linewidth=2.5, edgecolor=colors[label],
               color=colors[label] if train_doc else "white")
    ax.annotate("D" + nodes.name.iloc[k].split("#")[1], xy, ha="center", va="center", zorder=3,
                fontsize=9, weight="bold", color="white" if train_doc else colors[label])

dense = adj.toarray()
dense = np.maximum(dense, dense.T)                              # undirected
colors = {"space": "tab:blue", "cooking": "tab:orange"}
WORD_FILL, WORD_EDGE = "#f2efe6", "#b8b2a0"

degree = (dense > 0).sum(axis=1)                                # number of edges per node
size = np.where(nodes.kind == "word", 100 + 45 * degree, 750)   # marker area in points²
radius = np.sqrt(size) / 2 / 72 * 0.33 * 1.6                    # approx. in layout units, with room for labels

# Lay out each connected component on its own and place them side by side,
# so that two topics with no shared words do not squeeze each other.
n_parts, part = connected_components(dense > 0, directed=False)
xy = np.zeros((len(dense), 2))
for p in range(n_parts):
    members = np.flatnonzero(part == p)
    local = force_layout(dense[np.ix_(members, members)] > 0, seed=p)
    local = (local - local.mean(axis=0)) / np.abs(local - local.mean(axis=0)).max()
    xy[members] = remove_overlaps(local, radius[members]) + [2.4 * p, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(22, 22))
for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(np.triu(dense))):
    ax.plot(*xy[[i, j]].T, color="gray", lw=0.4, alpha=0.5, zorder=0)
for k, name in enumerate(nodes.name):
    if nodes.kind.iloc[k] == "word":
        ax.scatter(*xy[k], s=size[k], color=WORD_FILL, edgecolor=WORD_EDGE, zorder=1)
        ax.annotate(name, xy[k], fontsize=7 + 0.25 * degree[k], ha="center", va="center", zorder=3)
    else:
        draw_document(ax, k, xy[k], size[k])

legend = [Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=12, color=c, label=f"{topic} document")
          for topic, c in colors.items()]
legend += [Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=12, mfc="white", mec="gray", mew=2,
                  label="test document (label hidden)"),
           Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=12, mfc=WORD_FILL, mec=WORD_EDGE,
                  label="word (size = number of edges)")]
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc="lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.08))
ax.set_title("The word-document graph of the toy corpus")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off");

    The two topics separate before any training. In this toy corpus they share no words at all, so they form two islands; in real corpora common words link the topics, and the edge weights carry the signal. Each test document (hollow) sits among the training documents of its topic, connected through shared words such as bread, chef or telescope.

    Zooming in: two hops from a test document¶

    The full drawing hides the edge weights. Let's zoom in on the first test document, "The chef baked fresh bread and served it with soup": its words, and the training documents that share at least one of them. These are exactly the nodes two hops away, the ones a 2-layer GCN mixes into its prediction.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch

target = n_train + n_words                                    # the first test document, as above
its_words = np.flatnonzero(dense[target])                     # one hop: its words
neighbours = [k for k in range(n_train) if dense[k, its_words].any()]  # two hops: docs sharing a word
sub = [*neighbours, *its_words, target]
sub_names = nodes.name.values[sub]
sub_adj = dense[np.ix_(sub, sub)]

# Three columns: training documents | words | test document.
column = {"train doc": 0, "word": 1, "test doc": 2}
xy_sub = np.zeros((len(sub), 2))
for kind, x in column.items():
    members = [k for k, node in enumerate(sub) if nodes.kind.iloc[node] == kind]
    xy_sub[members] = [(x, y) for y in np.linspace(1, -1, len(members) + 2)[1:-1]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 8))
for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(np.triu(sub_adj))):
    pmi = nodes.kind.iloc[sub[i]] == nodes.kind.iloc[sub[j]] == "word"
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy_sub[i], xy_sub[j], arrowstyle="-", zorder=0,
                                 connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.6" if pmi else "arc3",
                                 color="silver" if pmi else "tab:green", lw=sub_adj[i, j] * 1.2))
for k, node in enumerate(sub):
    if nodes.kind.iloc[node] == "word":
        ax.annotate(nodes.name.iloc[node], xy_sub[k], fontsize=11, ha="center", va="center",
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc=WORD_FILL, ec=WORD_EDGE))
    else:
        draw_document(ax, node, xy_sub[k], size=900)
for kind, x in column.items():
    ax.text(x, 1.02, {"train doc": "training documents", "word": "its words",
                      "test doc": "test document"}[kind], ha="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
ax.set(xlim=(-0.4, 2.4), ylim=(-1, 1.1))
ax.set_title("Two hops from a test document (green: TF-IDF, grey: PMI; width = weight)", pad=12)
ax.axis("off");
    from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch target = n_train + n_words # the first test document, as above its_words = np.flatnonzero(dense[target]) # one hop: its words neighbours = [k for k in range(n_train) if dense[k, its_words].any()] # two hops: docs sharing a word sub = [*neighbours, *its_words, target] sub_names = nodes.name.values[sub] sub_adj = dense[np.ix_(sub, sub)] # Three columns: training documents | words | test document. column = {"train doc": 0, "word": 1, "test doc": 2} xy_sub = np.zeros((len(sub), 2)) for kind, x in column.items(): members = [k for k, node in enumerate(sub) if nodes.kind.iloc[node] == kind] xy_sub[members] = [(x, y) for y in np.linspace(1, -1, len(members) + 2)[1:-1]] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 8)) for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(np.triu(sub_adj))): pmi = nodes.kind.iloc[sub[i]] == nodes.kind.iloc[sub[j]] == "word" ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy_sub[i], xy_sub[j], arrowstyle="-", zorder=0, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.6" if pmi else "arc3", color="silver" if pmi else "tab:green", lw=sub_adj[i, j] * 1.2)) for k, node in enumerate(sub): if nodes.kind.iloc[node] == "word": ax.annotate(nodes.name.iloc[node], xy_sub[k], fontsize=11, ha="center", va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc=WORD_FILL, ec=WORD_EDGE)) else: draw_document(ax, node, xy_sub[k], size=900) for kind, x in column.items(): ax.text(x, 1.02, {"train doc": "training documents", "word": "its words", "test doc": "test document"}[kind], ha="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold") ax.set(xlim=(-0.4, 2.4), ylim=(-1, 1.1)) ax.set_title("Two hops from a test document (green: TF-IDF, grey: PMI; width = weight)", pad=12) ax.axis("off");

    Every path from a training document to the test document goes through a word. A training document that shares three words with it has three paths; the others have one each. The grey arcs are the PMI edges between the words themselves.

    The same graph as a matrix¶

    The GCN never sees a drawing. It sees the adjacency matrix $A$, where $A_{ij}$ is the weight of the edge between nodes $i$ and $j$, or zero if there is none. Rows and columns follow the node order above, so the matrix splits into blocks:

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 12))
image = ax.imshow(np.ma.masked_equal(dense, 0), cmap="Oranges")    # blank cell = no edge
for border in (n_train - 0.5, n_train + n_words - 0.5):
    ax.axhline(border, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.axvline(border, color="black", lw=0.8)
ticks = [n_train / 2, n_train + n_words / 2, n_train + n_words + len(test) / 2]
ax.set_xticks(ticks, ["train\ndocs", "words", "test\ndocs"])
ax.set_yticks(ticks, ["train docs", "words", "test docs"], rotation=90, va="center")
ax.tick_params(length=0)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, shrink=0.75, label="edge weight")
ax.set_title(f"Adjacency matrix A: {len(dense)}×{len(dense)}, "
             f"{np.count_nonzero(dense) / dense.size:.0%} non-zero");
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 12)) image = ax.imshow(np.ma.masked_equal(dense, 0), cmap="Oranges") # blank cell = no edge for border in (n_train - 0.5, n_train + n_words - 0.5): ax.axhline(border, color="black", lw=0.8) ax.axvline(border, color="black", lw=0.8) ticks = [n_train / 2, n_train + n_words / 2, n_train + n_words + len(test) / 2] ax.set_xticks(ticks, ["train\ndocs", "words", "test\ndocs"]) ax.set_yticks(ticks, ["train docs", "words", "test docs"], rotation=90, va="center") ax.tick_params(length=0) fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, shrink=0.75, label="edge weight") ax.set_title(f"Adjacency matrix A: {len(dense)}×{len(dense)}, " f"{np.count_nonzero(dense) / dense.size:.0%} non-zero");
    • words $\times$ words: PMI edges. The vocabulary is listed in order of first appearance, so the words of one sentence sit next to each other and form the dark squares along the diagonal.
    • documents $\times$ words (and its mirror image, since $A$ is symmetric): TF-IDF edges, one per word the document contains.
    • documents $\times$ documents: empty. Documents only meet through words, as the zoom showed.
    • The diagonal is zero. Self-loops are added later, when $A$ is normalised.

    Even this toy matrix is mostly zeros. In a real corpus almost every entry is zero, which is why Text4GCN stores $A$ as a scipy.sparse matrix.

    Here is the zoomed-in neighbourhood as rows and columns of $A$. Read a row to get a node's edges: the test document's row holds the TF-IDF weights of its words, and its cells against the training documents are empty.

    Why this helps: labels travel along edges¶

    A 2-layer GCN computes

    $$\hat{A} \cdot \mathrm{ReLU}(\hat{A} \cdot X \cdot W_1) \cdot W_2, \qquad \hat{A} = D^{-1/2} (A + I) \, D^{-1/2}$$

    where $X$ holds the node features and $W_1$, $W_2$ are the learned weights. $\hat{A}$ is the normalised adjacency: self-loops are added ($A + I$), and every weight is divided by the square root of the weighted degrees $D$ of its two nodes. Every layer mixes each node with its neighbours, so after two layers a document has heard from its words and from the other documents that share those words.

    The same neighbourhood in $\hat{A}$:

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    a_hat = dense + np.eye(len(dense)) # self-loops
d = a_hat.sum(axis=1)
a_hat = a_hat / np.sqrt(np.outer(d, d)) # D^-1/2 (A + I) D^-1/2

show_matrix(a_hat, "Greens")
    a_hat = dense + np.eye(len(dense)) # self-loops d = a_hat.sum(axis=1) a_hat = a_hat / np.sqrt(np.outer(d, d)) # D^-1/2 (A + I) D^-1/2 show_matrix(a_hat, "Greens")

    cooking doc #9 0.06 0.07

    fresh 0.07 0.08 0.01 0.04 0.07 0.07 0.08 0.08 0.08
    chef 0.11 0.03 0.07 0.06 0.10 0.12 0.12 0.12
    soup 0.11 0.03 0.07 0.10 0.06 0.12 0.12 0.12

    Two things changed from $A$. The diagonal is filled, so each node keeps part of its own features at every layer. And the weights shrink, most of all for nodes with many strong edges. bread and fresh also appear in other documents, so they drop from 1.39 to 0.08. baked and served appear only here and keep the strongest links to the test document. A well-connected word is a weaker clue about any single document.

    We can see the effect without any learning. Spread the one-hot labels of the training documents over two hops ($\hat{A}^2 \cdot Y$) and read the scores of the test documents:

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    classes = sorted(colors)
y = np.zeros((len(dense), len(classes)))
for k, label in enumerate(train.label):
    y[k, classes.index(label)] = 1.0          # only training documents carry a label

scores = a_hat @ a_hat @ y                    # two hops of propagation
test_rows = range(n_train + n_words, len(dense))
pd.DataFrame(scores[test_rows], columns=classes,
             index=[f"{lb} (true)" for lb in test.label]).round(3)
    classes = sorted(colors) y = np.zeros((len(dense), len(classes))) for k, label in enumerate(train.label): y[k, classes.index(label)] = 1.0 # only training documents carry a label scores = a_hat @ a_hat @ y # two hops of propagation test_rows = range(n_train + n_words, len(dense)) pd.DataFrame(scores[test_rows], columns=classes, index=[f"{lb} (true)" for lb in test.label]).round(3)
    Out[15]:
    cooking space
    cooking (true) 0.052 0.000
    space (true) 0.000 0.082

    Each test document gets the higher score for its true topic. The labels reached it through the graph.

    A GCN learns how much each hop and each feature should count, instead of using fixed weights. Because test documents are nodes of the same graph, the model is transductive: classifying a new document means adding it to the graph and training again.
